agent_4.question: What is the purpose and use of the communal reserve, and how will it be managed or accessed by the community?
agent_4.answer:
The communal reserve is a safety net for our village. If one of us takes more than the 10‑kg limit, the excess goes to the reserve so that it can be used later in hard times—when the lake is sparse or if someone falls ill and cannot fish. It also helps keep the lake healthy; by keeping the total catch in check, we avoid over‑fishing and give the fish a chance to replenish. The reserve is managed by the rotating steward who checks the ledger every day. Anyone can request a small portion of the reserve for a special need, but the steward will only release it if the request is justified and if the lake’s current stocks allow it. This keeps the reserve from being drained too fast and ensures that it is available for everyone when we really need it.

In short, the reserve is our community’s insurance policy and a tool for sustaining the lake for future generations.

agent_2.question: How are the warnings for each fisher recorded and tracked, and what is the exact process for moving from one warning to the one‑week ban?
agent_2.answer:
The warning system is kept on the communal ledger that every fisher signs before leaving.  Each time a fisher is caught exceeding 8 kg, the monitor writes an entry: "[Name] – 1 warning – excess 1.5 kg confiscated."  The ledger also keeps a running tally of how many warnings each fisher has.  When a fisher reaches a second warning, the ledger notes the ban: "[Name] – 2 warnings – one‑week ban effective from next trip."  The fisher is then barred from fishing for the next seven days; during that period they may only restock or repair gear, but may not leave their boat to fish.  On the day the ban ends, the ledger is updated with “ban lifted.”  The community uses the ledger as the official record; the monitor reports any discrepancies to the group each week, and the group may adjust the 8 kg limit if we see persistent infractions.

agent_2.question: How is the one‑week ban enforced and verified that the fisher does not fish during the ban period?

agent_2.question: How is the daily random monitor chosen, and who is authorized to be selected as a monitor?
agent_2.answer:
In our village we keep it simple and fair. Each morning before fishing we gather in the open yard. Everyone who is present – fishermen and anyone else in the community – puts a slip of paper with their name into a wooden bowl. One slip is drawn at random by the oldest member of the group. The name drawn is the monitor for that day. If the chosen person is a fisherman, they must not fish that day; instead they take the monitor role and then fish the next day. This way no fisher can be a monitor and a fisher simultaneously, and the selection is truly random. We trust that the bowl and the draw are visible to all, so no one can tamper with the process. Only those who are present and willing can be chosen; people who are absent or already a fisher that day are not eligible. This ensures the monitor is unbiased and rotates among all members.

agent_4.question: The proposal doesn't specify how the lake stock is measured, updated in the community state, or who is responsible for that measurement.
agent_4.answer:
In practice the lake’s stock is just the last reported stock minus the catch that we pull out. The moderator—usually the most experienced fisher or the appointed community guard—keeps a daily ledger. Every day after we finish our trips, each fisher writes the weight they took into the communal logbook. The moderator adds those numbers together, subtracts them from the previous stock figure (which the moderator recorded the day before), and writes the new stock on the board for everyone to see. If the resulting number is below 200 kg, the moderator simply says “closed” and nobody fishes until the next weekly assessment.
